_about: The outer skin (hull agent). hull.js reads this file. materials: the skin materials a section may use, the first is the default. costPerM2 is in game dollars, scaled like the rest of the catalogue (a crew capsule costs $380k here), not real prices; strengthKPa is a game rating (see physics._about). physics: the constants of the simple skin models (mass, heat on the climb, buckling at Max-Q, drag), each with its source. profiles: how hull.js sees each axial part from outside (shell = its wall is the outer skin, inner = narrower hardware the skin must cover, own = keeps its own shape, cover = a nose cover that may enclose a capsule as a fairing, tower = escape tower, engine). inside: which side-mounted parts ride inside the skin, and where. Numbers marked 'TODO verify' are game estimates still to check against a primary source.

materials.name: Aluminium 2219 skin
materials.note: The classic rocket aluminium: a thin welded and riveted skin with stiffening ribs inside. Not the lightest, but strong, cheap enough, and happy up to about 200 °C on the climb.
cons: Rivet heads add a little drag
materials.real: Saturn V S-IC tanks and the Space Shuttle's Standard Weight external tank
sources: toughness 1 (1 = 2219 skin): the energy that holes this skin over that of 2219's, the reference: a 2.5 mm 2219 sheet; Cour-Palais single-wall equation for sheets, Christiansen's Whipple equation with the core gap counted at a quarter for sandwiches (NASA TP-2003-210788, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030068423; src/builder/traits/structure.json)
Density 2.84 g/cm3, tensile 172-476 MPa; used for the Shuttle Standard Weight Tank: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2219_aluminium_alloy

Developed for service up to 600 F (316 C), with good tensile, fatigue and creep properties up to that temperature: NASA Materials Data Handbook, Aluminum Alloy 2219 (1966), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19660015199
S-IC propellant tanks built from 2219 aluminium panels: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-IC

massPerM2 9: a 2.5 mm skin (7.1 kg/m2) with light stringers and frames; the skin here is an aerodynamic cover over parts that already carry the loads, so fairing-panel weight, not load-carrying interstage weight (hull agent estimate, TODO verify)
maxTempC 200: well below the 316 C handbook figure; 2219-T87 keeps most of its strength after minutes at 200 C (TODO verify the exact knock-down)
strengthKPa 58 (game rating): a 2219 skin-stringer panel sized to meet the crewed factor of safety 1.4 at the flight model’s 40 kPa limit, with a little margin

materials.name: Aluminium-lithium 2195 skin
materials.note: A pinch of lithium makes aluminium a little lighter and stiffer and about 30 % stronger. For a skin, though, stiffness (not strength) sets how thin it can be, so it saves only about 6 % here. It costs more and does not like heat above about 150 °C.
pros: About 6 % lighter than 2219 for the same stiffness
cons: Loses strength above about 150 °C: near the nose it can run hot
materials.real: Space Shuttle Super Lightweight Tank (1998), Falcon 9 tank walls and domes
sources: toughness 1.13 (1 = 2219 skin): the energy that holes this skin over that of 2219's, a 2.45 mm 2195 sheet, harder and stiffer than 2219; Cour-Palais single-wall equation for sheets, Christiansen's Whipple equation with the core gap counted at a quarter for sandwiches (NASA TP-2003-210788, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030068423; src/builder/traits/structure.json)

2195 is 30 % stronger and 5 % less dense than 2219; the Super Lightweight Tank was 7,500 lb lighter, first flew on STS-91 in June 1998: NASA fact sheet https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/113020main_shuttle_lightweight.pdf
Falcon 9 propellant tank walls and domes are aluminium-lithium; boosters have flown up to 37 times: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9
Al-Li strength falls above about 150 C as its strengthening particles coarsen (TODO verify with a 2195 datasheet)
specificHeat 880 J/kg/K: TODO verify

massPerM2 8.4 and strengthKPa 57 (game rating): for a buckling-critical skin the thickness goes as sqrt(load / E); with E 76 GPa vs 73 GPa and density 2,710 vs 2,840 kg/m3 the same buckling load needs 3.1 mm, 8.4 kg/m2 (about 6 % lighter than 2219), so its rating stays just below 2219’s

materials.name: Carbon-fibre sandwich skin
materials.note: Thin carbon-fibre sheets glued on both sides of an aluminium honeycomb: very stiff for its weight, but the resin softens above about 170 °C and it is expensive to make.
pros: Very stiff, so it shrugs off Max-Q
Smooth moulded surface, a little less drag
cons: Nearly three times the price of 2219
Resin softens above about 170 °C: near the nose it can run hot
materials.real: Falcon 9 interstage and payload fairing, Rocket Lab Electron, Delta IV interstages and fairings
sources: toughness 0.16 (1 = 2219 skin): the energy that holes this skin over that of 2219's, two 0.6 mm carbon faces on a 25 mm core: thin brittle faces are holed easily; Cour-Palais single-wall equation for sheets, Christiansen's Whipple equation with the core gap counted at a quarter for sandwiches (NASA TP-2003-210788, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030068423; src/builder/traits/structure.json)
Falcon 9 interstage: carbon-fibre aluminium-core composite; fairing: carbon fibre skin over an aluminium honeycomb core: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9

180 C-cure aerospace epoxies reach Tg 190-220 C dry and serve to about 150 C continuously (about 125 C when wet): resin suppliers' guides and patents, e.g. https://incurelab.com/wp/high-temperature-epoxy-laminating-resin; the game allows 170 C for the few dry minutes of the climb (TODO verify with a prepreg datasheet)

massPerM2 6: two 0.6 mm carbon face sheets, a 25 mm aluminium honeycomb core and adhesive (about 4 kg/m2) plus frames; a whole Falcon 9 fairing with its separation system is roughly 8 kg/m2 (TODO verify)
strengthKPa 62 (game rating): a sandwich panel’s bending stiffness grows with the square of its thickness, so for its weight it resists buckling far better than a solid sheet

materials.name: Stainless steel skin
materials.note: Welded rings of thin stainless steel: cheap, tough when frozen or hot, and good for many flights. It is the heaviest skin, and a thin steel wall is the least stiff for its weight.
pros: Shrugs off heat up to about 650 °C
Wears slowly: best for reusing the ship
cons: Least stiff for its weight: a small chance it wrinkles at Max-Q
materials.real: SpaceX Starship (304L, then 30X), Atlas and Centaur balloon tanks
sources: toughness 2.54 (1 = 2219 skin): the energy that holes this skin over that of 2219's, a 1.8 mm sheet of hard, dense steel; Cour-Palais single-wall equation for sheets, Christiansen's Whipple equation with the core gap counted at a quarter for sandwiches (NASA TP-2003-210788, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030068423; src/builder/traits/structure.json)

Starship stages are welded stainless steel rings 1.83 m tall and 3.97 mm thick; 304L on SN7, later a proprietary 30X; chosen for low cost, cryogenic strength and heat tolerance: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Starship
Atlas balloon tanks: stainless steel 0.36-0.94 mm thick, collapsed unless kept pressurised: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balloon_tank and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SM-65_Atlas
massPerM2 14.5: a 1.8 mm stainless sheet (14.4 kg/m2); E = 193 GPa, density 7,900 kg/m3
maxTempC 650: 304 stainless resists scaling to about 870 C in intermittent service but loses strength above about 550-650 C (TODO verify)
strengthKPa 51 (game rating): thin-shell buckling load per square metre goes as E (m/rho)^2: 193 GPa x (14.5/7,900)^2 is about 0.89 of 2219’s 73 GPa x (9/2,840)^2, so 0.89 x 58 kPa

materials.name: Aluminium honeycomb sandwich
materials.note: Two thin aluminium sheets glued to a honeycomb core, like a very strong cardboard. Light and cheap for its stiffness, but the glue limits heat and the bonds slowly let go flight after flight.
pros: Light: a little more than carbon
A sandwich is very stiff: it resists buckling well
cons: Thin face sheets warm up fast, and the glue softens near 150 °C
Bonds tire quickly: poor for reuse
Slightly weaker joints than solid metal
materials.real: Saturn IB and Saturn V Instrument Unit, Apollo spacecraft structure
sources: toughness 1.49 (1 = 2219 skin): the energy that holes this skin over that of 2219's, two 0.8 mm aluminium faces on a 25 mm core: the front face breaks the particle up like a small Whipple shield; Cour-Palais single-wall equation for sheets, Christiansen's Whipple equation with the core gap counted at a quarter for sandwiches (NASA TP-2003-210788, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030068423; src/builder/traits/structure.json)
Saturn V Instrument Unit: a ring of aluminium honeycomb sandwich 6.6 m across: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V_instrument_unit
maxTempC 150: high-temperature epoxy film adhesives for honeycomb serve to about 150 C (TODO verify)
fatiguePerFlight 0.08: bonded sandwich panels disbond and take in water with repeated thermal and pressure cycles (game estimate)
strengthKPa 60 (game rating): a honeycomb sandwich exists to resist buckling; its weak points are heat (the glue) and wear (disbonds), not stiffness

materials.name: Titanium Ti-6Al-4V skin
materials.note: Thin titanium alloy sheet with stiffening ribs: the metal of the SR-71 Blackbird's skin. It keeps its strength to about 400 °C, wears very slowly and stops debris better than aluminium of its thickness. For a skin that must not buckle it is no lighter, though: titanium is no stiffer for its weight, so the same stiffness takes about a quarter more mass. It is hard to form and weld, so it is the dearest skin.
pros: Wears very slowly: good for flying the ship again
Takes debris hits better than aluminium
cons: About 25 % heavier than 2219 for the same stiffness
The most expensive skin: hard to form and weld
Against debris the tanks' own metal matters more: the skin covers little of them
materials.real: Lockheed A-12 and SR-71 Blackbird skins (titanium was about 85-93 % of the airframe); the titanium inner pressure shells of the Mercury and Gemini cabins (their outer shingles were René 41 nickel alloy)
sources: Ti-6Al-4V (annealed): density 4.43 g/cm3, E 113.8 GPa, tensile about 950 MPa, yield about 880 MPa, specific heat 526 J/kg/K, used to about 400 C: ASM Aerospace Specification Metals datasheet https://asm.matweb.com/search/SpecificMaterial.asp?bassnum=mtp641 and MMPDS Ti-6Al-4V chapter

SR-71 / A-12: titanium alloy skin and structure (mostly Ti-13V-11Cr-3Al, about 85-93 % of the airframe), skin temperatures about 260-315 C at Mach 3.2: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird and NASA Dryden SR-71 fact sheet https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/armstrong/sr-71-blackbird/
Mercury and Gemini: titanium inner pressure vessel under René 41 outer shingles: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_spacecraft

massPerM2 11.2: a buckling-critical skin needs thickness ~ sqrt(1/E), so a 2.0 mm titanium sheet (2.5 x sqrt(73/114)) with ribs: 9 x (4430/2840) x sqrt(73.1/113.8) = 11.2 kg/m2; titanium is no stiffer per kg than aluminium (E/rho is about 25.7 for both), so the same stiffness costs mass (structure agent estimate)
strengthKPa 58 (game rating): the same thin-shell buckling rule as the others, E (m/rho)^2: 114 GPa x (11.2/4430)^2 is 0.99 of 2219’s 73 GPa x (9/2840)^2
maxTempC 400: Ti-6Al-4V keeps about 65 % of its room-temperature yield at 400 C and is used to about 400 C in service (MMPDS elevated-temperature curves; the SR-71 skin ran to about 315 C)
fatiguePerFlight 0.01: Ti-6Al-4V keeps about 55 % of its tensile strength as fatigue strength at 10^7 cycles, 2219-T87 about 25 % (MMPDS, ASM Handbook vol. 19); a quarter of 2219’s 0.04 (estimate)
costPerM2 9,000 (game dollars): titanium sheet costs several times aluminium per kilogram and must be formed hot and welded in inert gas (estimate, the dearest skin)

toughness 1.52 (1 = 2219 skin): the energy that holes the 2.0 mm sheet over that of the 2.5 mm 2219 sheet, from the Cour-Palais single-wall equation with the titanium correction of Ratliff, Christiansen and Bryant (NASA JSC, 2009): src/builder/traits/structure.json

physics._about: Simple, honest models. Mass and cost: skin area times the material's mass and price per square metre (the skin is an aerodynamic cover over parts that already carry the loads; prices are game dollars). Heat: a thin skin x metres behind the nose tip is heated along the game's own climb (ascent: [t s, altitude m, speed m/s], the Reliable preset on the flight's ascent guide, the same climb src/flight/effects/structure.js heats the skin on) by the boundary layer (flat plate: laminar Stanton number 0.332 Re_x^-0.5 Pr^-2/3 below transitionRe, turbulent 0.0296 Re_x^-0.2 Pr^-2/3 above it; adiabatic wall temperature with recovery factor 0.89) in the US Standard Atmosphere 1976 (atmosphere: [altitude m, density kg/m3, temperature K], interpolated, density in log) and cooled by its own radiation (emissivity). Where real rockets put cork the heating is higher, so a forward-facing cone (a flare that widens towards the tail) heats (1 + flareHeatK sin(half-angle)) times faster and a payload fairing's shoulder, just behind the nose cover, shoulderHeat times faster, both ramping in between Mach 1 and 2 (engineering estimates, TODO verify). The peak temperature is compared with the material's limit: no chance below the limit minus heatMarginC, then heatMax x (over / heatSpanC)^1.5. A flare or shoulder that would come within cork.triggerMarginC of that margin gets cork, as real ones do (its mass and price are added, and the skin under it stays cool: about 79 C instead of about 166 C on the flare under the Reliable capsule). With that, the default 2219 skin is at least 51 C below its 200 C limit everywhere on the four presets (hottest: about 149 C on Workhorse). With laminar flow near the nose and a turbulent boundary layer further aft, the plain skin is coolest about 2 m behind the tip and warmest about 8-10 m back. Max-Q: each material's strengthKPa is a game rating, the dynamic pressure its standard skin takes before it wrinkles, set from the thin-shell buckling rule (load per square metre goes as E (m/rho)^2 for solid sheets; sandwiches are stiffer). At or above safeFactor x maxQLimitKPa (1.4, the crewed ultimate factor of safety of NASA-STD-5001, as the ship carries a crew) there is no chance of buckling; below it the chance grows as buckleMax x ((safeFactor - S/limit) / buckleSpan)^buckleExp, scaled by how much skin there is (0.4 + area / buckleAreaRef, at most 1). Drag: the steps and open structures of the bare stack add drag area to the nose's (noseCdA); skin cones take most of it away; cdAFactor = clamp((nose + skinned steps) / (nose + bare steps), minFactor, maxFactor) x the skins' surface finish. Equipment boxes are not counted either way: the game's drag never charged them.
sources: Flight model limit 40 kPa: src/flight/FlightController.js TUNING.maxQ ('real rockets see ~30-35 kPa at Max-Q')
Space Shuttle max q about 0.32 atm at about 11 km; Apollo just over 0.3 atm at 13-14 km: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_q
US Standard Atmosphere 1976 (NOAA/NASA/USAF): density and temperature by altitude, to 100 km, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19770009539

Turbulent flat-plate heat transfer: Stanton number about 0.0296 Re_x^-0.2 Pr^-2/3 (Colburn analogy), recovery factor about Pr^1/3 = 0.89 (standard boundary-layer results, e.g. Incropera, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer)

Laminar flat plate below transitionRe = 5 x 10^5 (the classic flat-plate transition Reynolds number): local Stanton number 0.332 Re_x^-1/2 Pr^-2/3 (Pohlhausen; Incropera ch. 7). High on the climb the air is thin and the Reynolds number falls below it: at 1.7 m behind the nose Re_x is about 3.7 x 10^5 at 44 km and 1.5 x 10^4 at 72 km on the game's climb, so the boundary layer there is laminar and heats about half as fast as a turbulent one (structure reviewer's measurement)

ascent: the game's own climb, so the hangar and the flight agree: the Reliable preset flown by the flight's ascent guide (src/flight/tests/paceSim.mjs simulateAscent), max-Q about 22 kPa at T+71 s near 11.8 km, then minutes near 2.2 km/s between 60 and 90 km (the 1/10-scale planet's orbit is 2.5 km/s), sampled to T+330 s (structure reviewer's measurement, wave 5). A real Falcon 9 reaches max-Q about T+72 s near 12 km and MECO about T+155 s near 68 km and 2.1 km/s

flareHeatK: compression on a flare raises the local pressure (Newtonian Cp = 2 sin^2 of the deflection) and turbulent heating goes roughly as density^0.8; a 30 degree flare at Mach 2-3 heats 2-3 times faster than a flat plate. Real flares and fairing noses carry cork: the Apollo spacecraft-LM adapter was cork-covered (TODO verify the factor)
safeFactor 1.4: NASA-STD-5001 (Structural Design and Test Factors of Safety for Spaceflight Hardware), ultimate factor of safety 1.4 for metallic flight structure on crewed vehicles

Drag: forward-facing step Cd about 0.9 and base drag about 0.25 of the annulus area; cones scale with sin^2 of their half-angle (Newtonian), boat-tails with sin (Hoerner, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, TODO verify the exact factors)

cork: a 6 mm cork sheet (P-50 class, about 0.48 g/cm3, so about 3 kg/m2, conductivity about 0.05 W/m/K, so a thermal resistance of about 0.12 m2K/W) glued over a flare or a fairing shoulder; the char layer takes the heat and the metal under it stays cool (TODO verify against a cork TPS datasheet). Apollo spacecraft-LM adapter, Atlas and Titan fairings carried cork

profiles._about: How the skin sees an axial part. Missing ids use the rules in hull.js: engines are 'engine', adapters 'adapter', capsules 'own', axial abort parts 'tower', everything else 'shell' (its wall is the outer skin). r* are fractions of the part's own radius; bareR is the effective radius of an open structure for the bare-stack drag; bt is a nose cover's boat-tail height (m) when it does not enclose a capsule; climb is how far (m) a skin cone may run up the base of an own-shape part.

inside._about: Side-mounted parts ride inside the skin (hidden while their card is closed, seen through the skin when it is open) unless they really live outside: strap-on boosters, fins and grid fins, landing legs, antennas, escape towers and abort pods, RCS pods, aft fairings, verniers, jet vanes, and the long external lines and protective shields that are themselves part of the outer surface. A part on a host that the skin covers completely (a capsule under a fairing) is inside whatever it is. alwaysInside overrides the outside rules (a relay satellite and airbags ride stowed; nitrogen spheres carry the rcs flag but are tanks). axis: parts drawn round the rocket's axis (seals in the joints, gimbal actuators at the engine); their ShipSpec position stays on the host's wall. Equipment is never put inside the propellant: an item clamped to a tank moves to the nearest dry bay (a skin bay, a dry structure such as an intertank or instrument ring, or a tank's forward or aft skirt, the dry ring between the dome and the wall, skirtFrac x the tank's radius tall and at most skirtDepth deep), and what fits nowhere goes into one automatic equipment bay (bay: a short cylinder of skin at the body's diameter; the items stand round its wall in rings, each ring as tall as its tallest item plus headroom, gap between neighbours, useOfRing of the circumference used, a frame at each end; minHeight..maxHeight tall, maxHeight 2.8 m because a stowed 2.4 m solar wing must fit). Where (prefer, the first that exists): intertank = next to a real intertank or centerbody right under the topmost tank (intertankMatch), where real intertanks carry avionics (Saturn V S-IC, Shuttle external tank), or else below that tank's own aft skirt, lattice or hung tank (stagePartMatch, or a tank hung inside a skirt), so it never splits a stage (S-IVB, S-II, DCSS, Blok I); nose = just under the capsule or payload, where service modules ride (Apollo SM, Orion ESM, Soyuz instrument compartment, Dragon trunk); otherwise on top of the topmost tank. intertank comes first because a bay up front puts more side area ahead of the centre of mass: on Reliable, Workhorse and Thin Skin it made the ship UNSTABLE (margin about -0.5 %), while under the top tank they keep about +4 %. tankSafe parts may stay in the tank: helium bottles really ride submerged in liquid oxygen on Falcon 9.
